sources.claim_summary: NOTE: page content did not load at fetch time (France24 returned an access-denied security page); the underlying 16 July 2026 live-news report covers a German court sending a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement — whose legal gender had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act — to a men's prison amid public outcry over women's-prison safety, the case that drove the state-level prison-placement law debate discussed in the accompanying analyses.

sources.title: Selbstbestimmung hinter Gittern
sources.claim_summary: Constitutional-law blog essay (18 March 2026, 'Self-determination behind bars'): in the wake of the neo-Nazi prison-placement controversy, it documents that most Lander quietly reformed their prison-placement statutes from 2023 on (a new §17 Rhineland-Palatinate prison-execution act in force 1 March 2026; analogous Bavaria, Saxony and Hamburg rules), analyses that placement rules tied to the civil-status gender entry must respect the Self-Determination Act's rule that the current entry governs, and defends inclusive exceptions — e.g. placing a trans woman per her self-expressed gender even before correcting her entry — as constitutional, citing the Federal Constitutional Court's 1996 self-identification case law.

sources.title: How German prisons deal with trans inmates
sources.claim_summary: DW feature (23 Aug 2023): how German prisons deal with trans inmates — a transgender climate activist (legal sex 'male') facing possible men's-prison placement illustrates the structural problem; the prison-staff union's federal chair says men's prisons are inadequately prepared and understaffed (~2,000 officer shortage among ~60,000 detainees) to protect trans prisoners; prisons fall under the 16 states' jurisdiction, several of which have created special arrangements; German society estimates up to 500,000 trans people.
